stem: A 28-year-old female patient is referred to a psychiatrist by her primary care physician due to a recent onset of episodes of altered behavior which last about one to two minutes at most. The patient's spouse notes that when these episodes occur while the patient is cooking, she will place all the clean silverware back in the dishwasher. During the episodes the spouse has observed the patient making chewing movements, and indicates that he is unable to interrupt the patient's behavior. After the episode, the patient has no recollection of the events. A magnetic resonance imaging scan is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Explanation: Complex Partial Seizures (Q3) Clues: brief 1–2 min spells of altered awareness + automatisms (chewing, reloading silverware), no memory afterward, can’t be interrupted = focal seizure with impaired awareness (temporal lobe), formerly “complex partial.”
A normal MRI does NOT rule it out — EEG is the diagnostic test.
Why not the others: Transient global amnesia = hours of memory loss, patient alert and asks repetitive questions. Fugue/dissociative = psychological, stress-linked, lasts longer. Peduncular hallucinosis = vivid visual hallucinations from a midbrain lesion.
Takeaway: repetitive, purposeless automatisms + amnesia for the event → think temporal lobe epilepsy.

stem: A 23-year-old patient with severe borderline personality disorder and more than 20 past suicide attempts presents for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). The therapist asks the patient for a commitment to refrain from self-harm behaviors for one year. The patient replies, "Oh, sure, that won't be a problem at all, believe me." Which of the following responses by the therapist would be most consistent with principles of DBT?

options.text: Insist that the patient endorse the agreement in writing
Suggest that the patient increase the duration of the commitment to two years
Draw the patient's attention to the fact that this commitment would be extremely difficult to abide by
Inform the patient that treatment will be terminated if any acts of self-harm occur within the next year
Praise the patient for the decision and emphasize that the therapist does indeed believe that the patient will refrain from self-harm

answer_text: Draw the patient's attention to the fact that this commitment would be extremely difficult to abide by
answer_raw: C. Draw the patient's attention to the fact that this commitment would be extremely difficult to abide by
explanation_text:
Explanation: Epigenetics & Maternal Care (Q5) Answer D: the effect works through DNA methylation that changes glucocorticoid receptor (GR) expression — not a change in the DNA sequence itself.
Mechanism: more maternal licking/grooming → less methylation of the GR gene in the pup’s hippocampus → more GR → stronger negative feedback on the HPA (stress) axis → a calmer, less stress-reactive adult.
This is epigenetic (gene expression dialed up/down) and reversible by environment — NOT an altered genetic code (rules out C) and not simply inherited DNA (rules out A).
Real-world: early nurturing biologically “sets” the stress thermostat — a model for how childhood environment shapes adult stress and mood.
Background: The Meaney “Licking & Grooming” Studies In the early 2000s, Michael Meaney and Moshe Szyf at McGill showed that rat pups raised by high licking/grooming mothers became calmer adults, while pups of low-grooming mothers were more anxious and stress-reactive.
Cross-fostering proved it was nurturing, not genes: pups born to anxious mothers but raised by attentive mothers grew up calm.
They traced the effect to methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene in the hippocampus — and remarkably showed it could be reversed in adult rats with agents that alter methylation.
Why it matters: this was landmark evidence that experience leaves chemical marks on DNA, helping launch the field of behavioral epigenetics and shaping how psychiatry understands early-life adversity.

A recently retired woman begins outpatient psychotherapy to help cope with several recent transitions in her life. She mentions regret that she did not pursue a graduate degree and instead "settled" for her ten-year job as an administrative assistant. She worries about her grown children, a son who lives with her and is not financially independent, and a daughter whom "I could have set on a better path." She would like to do something meaningful in the last few decades of her life, but is unsure of her next step. Which of the following stages of psychosocial development is characterized by this patient?
In social psychology, the occurrence of a contradiction between two attitudes or between an attitude and a behavior is referred to as:
explanation_text:
Explanation: Carbamazepine + Erythromycin (Q7) Answer E: Carbamazepine. The clue is new toxicity (nausea, ataxia, diplopia) appearing right after erythromycin is added.
Why: carbamazepine is broken down by the liver enzyme CYP3A4. Erythromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, so carbamazepine isn’t cleared → levels rise → classic dose-related toxicity (ataxia, diplopia, nausea, drowsiness).
Bonus board facts: carbamazepine induces its own metabolism (autoinduction) and lowers levels of many drugs, including oral contraceptives.
Real-world: in any patient on carbamazepine, check for CYP3A4 interactions before adding antibiotics or antifungals.
Explanation: Erikson — Integrity vs. Despair (Q8) Answer C: Ego integrity vs. despair — Erikson’s final stage (late adulthood).
The clue is a backward life review: she weighs regrets (“settled” for her job, “could have set them on a better path”) and asks whether her life had meaning. Looking back and appraising one’s whole life is the hallmark of this stage.
Integrity = accepting your life as meaningful and well-lived; despair = bitterness and regret over missed chances.
Contrast with generativity vs. stagnation (midlife), which is about actively contributing — mentoring, raising children, producing — looking forward rather than reviewing the past.
Background: Erikson’s 8 Psychosocial Stages Trust vs. mistrust (infancy) 2. Autonomy vs. shame/doubt (toddler) 3. Initiative vs. guilt (preschool) 4. Industry vs. inferiority (school age) 5. Identity vs. role confusion (adolescence) 6. Intimacy vs. isolation (young adult) 7. Generativity vs. stagnation (midlife) 8. Ego integrity vs. despair (late life)
Each stage is a “crisis” to resolve; success builds a virtue (hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom).
High-yield tip: match the patient’s AGE and whether they’re looking forward (building/contributing) vs. backward (reviewing) to pick the stage.

stem: During a neurological exam a patient is unable to see objects presented in the upper left quadrant of each eye. This indicates a lesion in which of the following regions of the brain?
answer_text: Right temporal lobe E. Right optic radiation
answer_raw: D. Right temporal lobe E. Right optic radiation
explanation_text:
Explanation: Visual Field Defects — “PITS” (Q12) The defect is loss of the upper-left quadrant in BOTH eyes = a left superior homonymous quadrantanopia. “Homonymous” (same side in both eyes) means the lesion sits behind the optic chiasm, on the RIGHT side of the brain.
Upper-field defects come from the TEMPORAL lobe: fibers from the lower retina loop forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) on their way to the occipital cortex. A right temporal lesion (Meyer’s loop = part of the right optic radiation) wipes out the left upper field — so both D and E are credited.
Mnemonic — PITS: Parietal lesions → Inferior field cuts; Temporal lesions → Superior field cuts.
Real-world: map the defect (which eyes, which quadrant) backward along the pathway to localize the lesion.
Visual Pathway: Localizing Field Defects (Q12)

explanation_text:
Explanation: Catatonia — Lorazepam First (Q13) Answer C: Lorazepam. Immobility, posturing, and echopraxia (mimicking the examiner’s movements) = catatonia, which is common in MOOD disorders (here, bipolar), not just schizophrenia.
First-line treatment is a benzodiazepine — the “lorazepam challenge”; a rapid response also helps confirm the diagnosis. ECT is the definitive next step if benzodiazepines fail or for malignant catatonia (with fever and autonomic instability).
Avoid antipsychotics like haloperidol when catatonia is suspected — they can worsen it and raise the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Real-world: a mute, immobile, or posturing patient → reach for lorazepam, not an antipsychotic.
Background: The Major Dementias at a Glance (Q14) Alzheimer disease: gradual short-term memory loss first; most common dementia.
Dementia with Lewy bodies (the answer): FLUCTUATING cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism (resting tremor, rigidity) early; often REM sleep behavior disorder; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics.
Vascular: stepwise decline linked to strokes and vascular risk factors.
Frontotemporal: early personality/behavior change or language loss, memory relatively spared, younger onset.
Prion (Creutzfeldt-Jakob): rapid dementia plus myoclonus over weeks to months.
Tip: identify the FIRST and most distinctive feature to tell them apart.

Explanation: Sleep in Depression — Short REM Latency (Q18) Answer A: Short REM latency. In major depression the brain reaches its first REM period unusually fast (the gap from falling asleep to REM is shortened).

Memory hook: in depression, REM comes “too soon and too much.”

Explanation: Lithium Toxicity (Q19) Answer C: Lithium. Clues: a bipolar patient who DOUBLED her dose, now with diarrhea, tremor, and confusion/disorientation — the classic picture of lithium toxicity.
Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window, so small dose increases (or anything that concentrates it) can tip a patient into toxicity. Early signs: coarse tremor, nausea/diarrhea, ataxia; severe: confusion, seizures, arrhythmia.
Watch the level-raising triggers: dehydration, low sodium, NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, and ACE inhibitors.
Real-world: new tremor + GI upset + confusion in someone on lithium → check a level and hold the dose.

A new instrument is developed to assess for posttraumatic stress disorder. The instrument covers intrusion, avoidance, arousal, and cognitive and mood symptoms, but it does not specifically inquire about the presence of a traumatic event. This omission raises concern about which of the following types of validity?
explanation_text:
Explanation: Content Validity (Q24) Answer A: Content validity — does the test actually cover the FULL concept it claims to measure? A PTSD scale that never asks about a traumatic event is missing a core piece of the disorder, so its content coverage is incomplete.
Quick contrasts: Criterion validity = agreement with a gold standard (concurrent = right now; predictive = a future outcome). Discriminant validity = it should NOT correlate with unrelated constructs.
Real-world: when test items fail to represent every key part of what you’re measuring, suspect a content-validity problem.
Background: Validity vs. Reliability (Q24) Reliability = consistency (same result on repeat). Types: test-retest (over time), inter-rater (between raters), internal consistency (items agree with each other).
Validity = accuracy (measures what it claims). Types: content (covers the whole concept), criterion (matches a gold standard — concurrent now or predictive later), construct (behaves as theory predicts), discriminant (doesn’t track unrelated things).
Key idea: a test can be reliable but not valid (consistently wrong), but it can’t be valid without being reliable.
Memory hook: reliability = the same; validity = the truth.

explanation_text:
Explanation: Klüver-Bucy Syndrome (Q27) Answer D: Temporal lobes. Bilateral damage to the anterior temporal lobes — especially the amygdala — produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome.
Classic features: placidity (tameness, loss of fear), hyperorality (examining things with the mouth), hypersexuality, and hyperphagia, plus visual agnosia (“psychic blindness”).
Why: the amygdala normally tags stimuli with emotional meaning; without it, fear and the ability to recognize the significance of what’s seen are lost.
Real-world: in humans it can follow herpes encephalitis, head trauma, or frontotemporal dementia — all of which strike the temporal lobes.

Explanation: Anorexia Nervosa vs. ARFID (Q28) Answer B: Anorexia nervosa. Key features: significant weight loss to a low weight (fell from the 75th to the 20th percentile), restricting intake, and preoccupation with food content — driven by body image (“self-conscious about appearance”) and a wish to lose more.
That body-image / fear-of-weight-gain motive is what makes it anorexia — not a “healthy eating approach” © and not ARFID (E).
ARFID is restriction WITHOUT any weight or shape concern (e.g., sensory aversion or fear of choking) — that’s the key separator.

Explanation: Orbitofrontal Syndrome (Q32) Answer D: Orbitofrontal cortex. After a head injury, the combination of impulsivity, euphoria, and disinhibition points to the orbitofrontal region.
The orbitofrontal cortex is the brain’s “brakes” on impulses and social behavior; damage releases those brakes → disinhibited, euphoric, socially inappropriate behavior (the classic Phineas Gage story).
Real-world: personality change + poor impulse control + a jokey or euphoric affect after frontal trauma = orbitofrontal damage.
Background: Three Frontal Lobe Syndromes (Q32) Orbitofrontal (disinhibited): impulsive, euphoric, socially inappropriate, poor judgment — “pseudopsychopathic.”
Dorsolateral (dysexecutive): poor planning, working memory, and mental flexibility — trouble organizing and problem-solving.
Medial frontal / anterior cingulate (apathetic): abulia — reduced motivation, spontaneity, and movement; in the extreme, akinetic mutism.
Tip: match the deficit — disinhibition vs. poor executive function vs. apathy — to the region.

The staff of a psychiatric unit contemplates an initiative aimed at reducing the risk for completed suicides in an inpatient setting. Which of the following interventions is likely to have the greatest effect on decreasing suicide risk while maintaining a therapeutic environment and minimizing staff burden?

options.text: Establishing "no-suicide" contracts which each patient at the time of admission
Redesigning the physical space to eliminate potential anchor points for hanging
Implementing the use of constant observation more frequently and for longer durations
Increasing the number of locked doors on a unit to decrease the risk of elopement
Adopting a "universal precautions" approach in which all patients are treated as being at risk for suicide

answer_text: Redesigning the physical space to eliminate potential anchor points for hanging
answer_raw: B. Redesigning the physical space to eliminate potential anchor points for hanging
explanation_text:
Explanation: Conversion (Functional Neurological) Disorder (Q34) Answer D: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder). Sudden vision loss with a NORMAL workup, and the patient steps around a garbage can — showing the visual system works even though she reports blindness.
Conversion disorder = genuine neurological symptoms (blindness, paralysis, nonepileptic seizures) that are incompatible with known disease and not consciously produced.
Key distinctions: it is NOT faking — factitious disorder and malingering involve intentional production (for the sick role or for external gain). Illness anxiety is fear of disease without an actual deficit.
Real-world: look for exam findings inconsistent with the claimed deficit (here, avoiding obstacles while “blind”).
Explanation: Inpatient Suicide Prevention (Q36) Answer B: Redesign the physical space to remove anchor points for hanging. Hanging/strangulation is the leading method of inpatient suicide, so removing fixtures (door hinges, hooks, bars) targets the most common means — the highest-impact “means restriction” strategy.
Why not the others: “no-suicide contracts” do NOT prevent suicide and can give false reassurance; constant observation is resource-heavy and hard to sustain; more locked doors and “treat everyone as high-risk” strain staff without targeting the actual method.
Real-world: the most effective inpatient safety move is environmental — design out the means.

A 72-year-old patient's examination is remarkable for profound sensory ataxia with loss of vibratory sensation and cognitive issues described as irritability fluctuating with somnolence. Which of the following is the most likely nutritional deficiency associated with these findings?
explanation_text:
Explanation: B12 (Cobalamin) Deficiency (Q39) Answer E: Cobalamin (vitamin B12). Sensory ataxia + loss of vibration/proprioception (dorsal columns) plus cognitive change = B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
“Combined” = dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception, sensory ataxia) AND lateral corticospinal tracts (weakness, spasticity, upgoing toes). B12 also causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropsychiatric symptoms (irritability, confusion — “megaloblastic madness”).
Always check B12 in older adults with unexplained gait + cognitive change — it’s treatable, and the nerve damage can become permanent if missed.
Contrast: thiamine (B1) → Wernicke; niacin (B3) → pellagra (the 3 D’s: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).

Contrast with ghrelin, the “hunger hormone” from the stomach that RISES before meals and drives appetite — leptin and ghrelin push in opposite directions.
Twist: most obesity involves leptin RESISTANCE (high leptin, but the brain stops responding), not a lack of leptin.

answer_raw: D. a "two-hit" model of pathogenesis exists in which predisposing environmental factors combine with genetic risk.
explanation_text:
Explanation: The “Two-Hit” (Gene + Environment) Model (Q60) Answer D: A two-hit model — genetic risk PLUS environmental factors. Identical (monozygotic) twins share ~100% of their genes, yet schizophrenia concordance is only ~50%. If genes alone caused it, identical twins would always match.
That gap means genes set susceptibility (the “first hit”), but environmental factors (obstetric complications, cannabis, urban upbringing, infections, stress) provide the “second hit” that triggers illness — the diathesis-stress idea.
Why not the others: the discordance is real (not a zygosity error, A), the unaffected twin usually won’t go on to develop it ©, and genes are clearly present (rules out E).
Real-world: psychiatric illness = genetic loading interacting with environment, almost never one alone.

Explanation: Fragile X Syndrome (Q62) Answer C: Fragile X — the most common INHERITED cause of intellectual disability. (Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause overall, but it’s usually a sporadic trisomy, not inherited.)
Fragile X comes from a CGG trinucleotide-repeat expansion that silences the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Boys are more affected; classic features include a long face, large ears, large testes (macroorchidism), and strong links to autism and ADHD.
Memory hook: “Fragile X = inherited; Down = most common overall.”

Explanation: Lithium + Thiazide Interaction (Q64) Answer B: Reduced renal clearance. Lithium is cleared entirely by the kidneys and is handled much like sodium. Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) make the kidney reabsorb more sodium — and lithium follows it — so lithium clearance falls and levels climb into the toxic range.
That’s why this patient, stable on lithium for years, developed tremor, ataxia, and GI symptoms soon after starting HCTZ.
Other level-raisers by the same volume/sodium logic: dehydration, a low-salt diet, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors.
Real-world: starting a thiazide (or any of these) in a lithium patient → anticipate a rising level and recheck it.

Explanation: Orexin (Hypocretin) & Narcolepsy (Q72) Answer A: Orexin A (hypocretin). Narcolepsy type 1 (with cataplexy) is caused by loss of orexin-producing neurons in the hypothalamus — thought to be autoimmune.
Orexin normally promotes wakefulness and stabilizes the sleep–wake boundary; without it, REM phenomena intrude into wakefulness → sleep attacks, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations.
Diagnosis: low orexin in the CSF; sleep studies show short REM latency (sleep-onset REM).
Real-world: think orexin loss when you see daytime sleep attacks plus cataplexy (sudden, emotion-triggered muscle weakness).

explanation_text:
Explanation: Agitation in Stimulant Intoxication (Q75) Answer A: Lorazepam. With suspected “bath salts” (synthetic cathinone) intoxication — agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, and fever — a benzodiazepine is first-line.
Benzodiazepines calm agitation, lower heart rate and blood pressure, reduce temperature, and protect against seizures — directly countering the sympathetic overdrive.
Avoid antipsychotics (haloperidol, ziprasidone, fluphenazine) as first-line here: they lower the seizure threshold, impair heat dissipation (worsening hyperthermia), and risk QT prolongation and dystonia. Metoclopramide shares those downsides.
Real-world: an agitated, hyperthermic, sympathetically driven patient → benzodiazepines first.

stem: Which of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors has the strongest association with birth defects?
explanation_text:
Explanation: Paroxetine in Pregnancy (Q78) Answer C: Paroxetine. Among SSRIs, paroxetine has the strongest link to birth defects — specifically cardiac malformations (e.g., septal defects) with first-trimester use; it historically carried a Category D warning.
Because of this, paroxetine is generally avoided in pregnancy and in women who may become pregnant; sertraline is often preferred when an SSRI is needed.
Also note: SSRIs late in pregnancy can cause a neonatal adaptation syndrome and a small risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.
Real-world: weigh the risks of untreated depression against medication risks — but if an SSRI is needed in pregnancy, avoid paroxetine.
Background: Freud’s Psychosexual Stages (Q76) Oral (0–1 yr): gratification through the mouth — feeding, biting.
Anal (1–3): control and toilet training; order vs. messiness.
Phallic (3–6): Oedipal/Electra conflict; identification with the same-sex parent.
Latency (6–puberty): sexual urges are dormant; energy goes into school, sports, and same-sex friendships — the boy focused on basketball who plays mostly with boys fits here.
Genital (puberty onward): mature sexual relationships.
Tip: Freud theorized that fixation at a stage shapes adult personality traits.

Over the next few days the symptoms worsen and he has severe constipation and progressive weakness of bulbar muscles. Sensation is normal and he is found to have pupils that do not react to light. explanation_text:
Explanation: Botulism (Q87) Answer D: Botulinum toxin. The clue is a DESCENDING paralysis that starts in the cranial nerves: blurry/double vision, ptosis, dysphagia, then bulbar weakness — plus fixed, dilated pupils, dry mouth, and constipation (autonomic/anticholinergic-type effects).
Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so muscles and parasympathetic synapses can’t fire — producing flaccid paralysis with NORMAL sensation.
Contrast: tetanus causes rigid/spastic paralysis (the opposite); Guillain-Barré is an ASCENDING paralysis.
Real-world: symmetric descending weakness + dilated unreactive pupils = botulism (in infants, the “floppy baby” from honey).

The picture: a school-age child with brief staring spells and eye fluttering lasting a few seconds, with no aura and no postictal confusion — the child simply “blanks out” and then resumes. Hyperventilation can provoke them.

explanation_text:
Explanation: Bitemporal Hemianopia — Optic Chiasm (Q96) Answer B: A lesion at the optic chiasm. At the chiasm, fibers from the NASAL half of each retina cross to the other side. Those nasal fibers carry the TEMPORAL (outer) visual fields, so a midline chiasm lesion wipes out both temporal fields — a bitemporal hemianopia (loss of peripheral vision on both sides).
Classic cause: a pituitary adenoma pressing up on the chiasm from below (also craniopharyngioma).
Localize by site: optic NERVE (A) → blindness in one eye; chiasm (B) → bitemporal hemianopia; optic TRACT © → contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Real-world: new bitemporal vision loss → image the pituitary/sella.

Explanation: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (Q102) Answer E: Porphobilinogen (in the urine). The triad of severe abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms (delirium, agitation), and peripheral neuropathy (limb weakness) — often with no clear surgical cause — points to acute intermittent porphyria (AIP).
AIP is a defect in heme synthesis; attacks build up porphyrin precursors including porphobilinogen, which spills into the urine (classically turning it dark/port-wine on standing).
Triggers: certain drugs, fasting, alcohol, and infection. Hyponatremia from SIADH is common during attacks.
Memory — the 5 P’s: Pain (abdominal), Polyneuropathy, Psych symptoms, Port-wine urine, Precipitated by drugs.

Explanation: Boundary Crossings vs. Violations (Q108) Answer C: Boundary violations are characteristically exploitative. A boundary CROSSING is a minor, often benign or even helpful deviation from the usual frame (a reassuring hug, a small gift, running late once) that doesn’t harm the patient.
A boundary VIOLATION harms or exploits the patient and serves the therapist’s needs — the clearest example being sexual contact, which is never acceptable.

Explanation: Addison Disease (Adrenal Insufficiency) (Q111) Answer D: Adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease). The combination — fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, nausea, hyperpigmentation, muscle cramps, plus a depressed/apathetic mood — is classic primary adrenal insufficiency.
Low cortisol and aldosterone cause fatigue, low sodium / high potassium (hence the salt craving), and low blood pressure. The hyperpigmentation comes from high ACTH driving melanocytes — a clue the problem is the adrenal gland itself (primary).
Psychiatric overlap: it can masquerade as depression, so it belongs on the “medical mimics” list.

Explanation: Fluvoxamine Raises Clozapine (Q117) Answer D: Fluvoxamine. Clozapine is metabolized mainly by the liver enzyme CYP1A2. stem: Which of the following regions of the central nervous system contain dopaminergic neurons which project to the caudate and putamen?
explanation_text:
Explanation: The Nigrostriatal Pathway (Q129) Answer D: Substantia nigra. Its dopaminergic neurons project to the caudate and putamen (the striatum) — the nigrostriatal pathway, which controls movement.
Degeneration here causes Parkinson’s disease; blocking these D2 receptors with antipsychotics causes drug-induced parkinsonism and other extrapyramidal side effects.
Contrast: the ventral tegmental area (VTA) is the source of the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine pathways (reward and cognition), not the striatal motor pathway.
Real-world: movement problems on antipsychotics trace back to nigrostriatal D2 blockade.
Background: The 4 Dopamine Pathways (Q129) Nigrostriatal (substantia nigra → striatum): movement; D2 blockade → extrapyramidal side effects / parkinsonism.
Mesolimbic (VTA → limbic system): too much dopamine = positive psychotic symptoms; antipsychotics block this to help.
Mesocortical (VTA → prefrontal cortex): too little = negative and cognitive symptoms.
Tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus → pituitary): dopamine normally suppresses prolactin; blockade → hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction).
Tip: an antipsychotic’s benefits AND side effects come from hitting all four pathways at once.

Explanation: Motivational Interviewing (Q141) Answer D: The therapist points out the discrepancy between the patient’s current behavior and their own goals/values, which motivates change. MI is collaborative and patient-centered — NOT directive or persuasive.

Explanation: Transient Global Amnesia (Q156) Answer C: Transient global amnesia (TGA). A sudden, isolated inability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia) lasting a few hours, with the patient ALERT, fluent, and otherwise intact — repeatedly asking the same orienting questions (“where are we going?”). Explanation: Lithium & ECT (Q174) Answer B: Lithium. Lithium should be held or reduced before ECT, because the combination raises the risk of prolonged seizures, post-ECT delirium/confusion, and neurotoxicity.

Real-world: review the med list before ECT — hold lithium, and minimize agents that interfere with inducing an adequate seizure.

stem: By which of the following mechanisms of action does phencyclidine induce psychosis?
explanation_text:
Explanation: PCP & the NMDA/Glutamate Model (Q180) Answer C: Inhibition of NMDA receptors. PCP (and ketamine) block the NMDA receptor channel — and at high doses this reproduces BOTH the positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia (hallucinations, paranoia, thought disorder, plus blunting and withdrawal).
This is the basis of the glutamate (NMDA-hypofunction) hypothesis of schizophrenia — a complement to the older dopamine hypothesis.
Tie-in: it’s the same receptor where glycine acts as a co-agonist (prior slide) and where memantine works in Alzheimer’s; ketamine’s rapid antidepressant effect also runs through NMDA.
Real-world: PCP intoxication can mimic acute psychosis — look for nystagmus, agitation, analgesia, and violence.

Explanation: QTc Prolongation (Q186) Answer E: Potassium channel blockade. Many antipsychotics block cardiac potassium channels (the hERG / IKr channel), which slows repolarization → a longer QT interval, raising the risk of torsades de pointes (a dangerous ventricular arrhythmia).
Higher-risk agents include ziprasidone, IV haloperidol, and thioridazine; risk grows with high doses, other QT-prolonging drugs, and low potassium or magnesium.
Practical step: check an ECG and correct electrolytes (K+, Mg2+) in at-risk patients.
Real-world: think “K+ channel block → long QT → torsades” — a key reason we monitor ECGs with certain antipsychotics.

A 52-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department with an acute change in mental status including confusion and fluctuating consciousness. A workup reveals pneumonia, and an antibiotic is initiated. Which of the following would be the most likely finding on electroencephalogram (EEG)?
answer_raw: E. Generalized theta and delta activity
explanation_text:
Explanation: EEG in Delirium (Q189) Answer E: Generalized theta and delta activity (diffuse slowing). Delirium — acute, fluctuating confusion from a medical cause (here, pneumonia/infection) — typically shows GENERALIZED slowing of the background rhythm on EEG.
This reflects globally impaired brain function and helps separate delirium from primary psychiatric illness, which usually has a normal EEG.
Contrasts: 3-Hz spike-and-wave = absence seizures; focal delta = a focal lesion; prominent beta = often a benzodiazepine/sedative effect.
Real-world: confused, inattentive, fluctuating patient + diffuse EEG slowing = delirium — find and treat the underlying medical cause.

Explanation: Describing Affect (Q194) Answer D: Constricted. The patient shows a REDUCED range and intensity of emotional expression — sad, soft-spoken, little smiling — but emotion still varies somewhat and prosody (vocal melody) is relatively normal. That mild reduction = constricted affect.

Speech is monotone, and the patient covers the ears at times during the interview, stating, "It is too loud." The patient denies that the cutting constituted a suicide attempt, but is unable to further elaborate, stating, "My parents can provide additional information." The parents report that the patient has always been noise intolerant as well as "quirky and socially awkward" but has appeared more withdrawn over the past three days since the parents announced a plan to separate. The patient has few friends, and prefers solitary activities. There is no previous history of self-injurious behavior. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Explanation: Autism Presenting as Self-Injury (Q198) Answer A: Autism spectrum disorder. The LIFELONG features give it away: poor eye contact, limited facial expression, monotone speech, stereotyped posturing, sensory hypersensitivity (“it’s too loud”), few friends, and a preference for solitary activity — present since childhood, not new.
The self-cutting here is NOT a suicide attempt; under stress (the parents’ separation), a person with autism may self-injure to cope with overwhelming emotion or sensory overload.
Why not the others: borderline PD involves identity/relationship instability (not lifelong social-communication deficits); social communication disorder lacks restricted/repetitive behaviors; MDD wouldn’t explain the lifelong pattern.
Real-world: anchor on the lifelong developmental pattern, and don’t assume self-injury always means suicidality.

Explanation: Genomic Imprinting (Q200) Answer A: Genomic imprinting. The phenotype depends on whether a gene/deletion is inherited from the FATHER or the MOTHER — because some genes are silenced (“imprinted”) based on parent of origin.

Explanation: Treating Cataplexy (Q203) Answer C: Venlafaxine. “Weakness in the arms and legs brought on by laughter” is cataplexy — sudden, emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone, the hallmark of narcolepsy type 1.
Cataplexy responds to antidepressants that boost norepinephrine/serotonin and SUPPRESS REM — SNRIs (venlafaxine), TCAs, and SSRIs; sodium oxybate is also used.
Note the split: stimulants and modafinil treat the daytime SLEEPINESS but don’t fix cataplexy — you need a REM-suppressing antidepressant for that.
Real-world: in narcolepsy, target sleepiness and cataplexy with different medications.

explanation_text:
Explanation: Trigeminal Neuralgia (Q210) Answer E: Carbamazepine. Brief, severe, electric “jabs” of facial pain in a trigeminal-nerve distribution, triggered by light touch — shaving, brushing teeth, chewing — with a normal MRI = classic trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux).
First-line treatment is carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine), which calms the hyperexcitable nerve firing; ordinary analgesics like opioids and NSAIDs don’t work well.
Contrast: sumatriptan treats migraine; indomethacin treats certain headache syndromes; steroids treat temporal arteritis.
Real-world: lightning-like, touch-triggered facial pain → think trigeminal neuralgia and reach for carbamazepine.

explanation_text:
Explanation: Functional (Psychogenic) Blindness (Q216) Answer C: Ocular jerk (nystagmus) when watching an optokinetic drum. Explanation: Hippocampus & Amnesia (Q220) Answer D: Amnesia. The hippocampus and parahippocampal region are essential for forming NEW long-term (declarative) memories. Contrast: derealization = the WORLD feels unreal, dreamlike, or distant. Easy hook: depersonalization = “I’m not real”; derealization = “the world isn’t real.”
These often occur together and are commonly triggered by acute stress, panic, trauma, or cannabis. An illusion is a misperceived REAL stimulus; hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations occur while falling asleep/waking.

When reviewing a set of extremely positive student evaluations a professor notes that one of them contains the comment, "could leave more time for questions during class." At a subsequent psychotherapy session the professor tells the psychiatrist, "I am a terrible professor. I just talk the whole time." This is an example of which of the following types of cognitive errors?
explanation_text:
Explanation: Selective Abstraction (Q226) Answer D: Selective abstraction — focusing on a single negative detail while ignoring the larger (positive) context. The professor fixates on one critical comment among glowing reviews and concludes “I’m a terrible professor.”
Contrast: personalization = blaming yourself for things outside your control; catastrophizing = expecting the worst outcome; arbitrary inference = drawing a conclusion with no evidence; dichotomous (all-or-nothing) thinking = seeing things as black or white.
Real-world: CBT helps patients notice they’re cherry-picking the negatives, then weigh the full evidence.
Background: Common Cognitive Distortions (Q226) All-or-nothing (dichotomous): seeing things in black-and-white extremes.
Overgeneralization: one bad event becomes a never-ending pattern.
Selective abstraction (mental filter): focusing only on the negatives.
Personalization: taking blame for things you didn’t cause.
Catastrophizing: assuming the worst-case outcome.
Arbitrary inference (jumping to conclusions): mind-reading or fortune-telling without evidence.
“Should” statements and labeling: rigid rules and harsh self-labels.
Tip: CBT = spot the distortion, then test it against the actual evidence.

Explanation: Attributable Risk (Q238) Answer D: Attributable risk. The DIFFERENCE between two incidence rates (28% − 16% = 12%) is the attributable risk (here, the absolute risk reduction) — how much risk the exposure/treatment adds or removes.
Contrast: relative risk is the RATIO of the rates (16% ÷ 28% ≈ 0.57), telling you risk in the treated group relative to placebo.
Bonus: number needed to treat = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction = 1 ÷ 0.12 ≈ 8 — treat about 8 patients to prevent one bad outcome.
Real-world: “difference” = absolute/attributable; “ratio” = relative — and NNT turns it into a clinical feel.
Background: Risk & Effect Measures (Q238) Absolute risk reduction (ARR): the difference in event rates between groups (here, 12%).
Relative risk (RR): ratio of risks (treated ÷ control); RR < 1 = protective.
Relative risk reduction (RRR): 1 − RR — how much the treatment cuts risk proportionally.
Number needed to treat (NNT): 1 ÷ ARR — patients treated to prevent one event (smaller is better).
Odds ratio (OR): used in case-control studies; approximates RR for rare outcomes.
Tip: relative measures can look impressive while the absolute benefit is small — always check the ARR and NNT.

Explanation: The OCD Loop — Cortico-Striatal-Thalamic Circuit (Q256) Answer A: Thalamus. The OCD “worry loop” is the cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit: orbitofrontal/anterior cingulate cortex → striatum (caudate) → thalamus → back to cortex. Real-world: OCD = a brain loop stuck in the “on” position.

Three self-object needs: MIRRORING (being affirmed/valued), IDEALIZING (looking up to a calm, strong figure), and TWINSHIP (feeling alike and belonging). Healthy development gradually internalizes these functions.
Clinical relevance: in narcissistic pathology the self leans heavily on others for esteem; therapy offers a reliable, empathic self-object experience to build a more cohesive self.
Real-world: a self-object is a person who props up your sense of self until you can do it yourself.

stem: Which of the following dopaminergic pathways includes the nucleus accumbens and mediates addiction and associated behaviors?
explanation_text:
Explanation: The Mesolimbic Pathway & Addiction (Q300) Answer A: Mesolimbic. This pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to the nucleus accumbens — the brain’s reward center — and is central to motivation, pleasure, and ADDICTION.
Nearly all drugs of abuse (and natural rewards) raise dopamine here; the accumbens reinforces the behavior, driving craving and compulsive use. Overactivity of this same pathway also underlies the POSITIVE symptoms of psychosis.
Recall the four dopamine pathways: mesolimbic (reward/psychosis), mesocortical (cognition/negative symptoms), nigrostriatal (movement), tuberoinfundibular (prolactin).
Real-world: “reward = mesolimbic” — the final common pathway for addiction, and a major target of antipsychotics.
